Task and constraints: Given an array of distinct integers candidates and a target integer target, return a list of all unique combinations of candidates where the chosen numbers sum to target. You may return the combinations in any order. Inputs and required output follow the stated problem constraints.
Idea: A mutable path and total are maintained. For each candidate from idx onward, the code appends it, recurses with the same index, then pops; it copies a path when total equals target and stops above target.
Technique and why it applies: Backtracking enumerates choices, and a nondecreasing index prevents permutation duplicates while permitting reuse.
Invariant: The path contains choices from the current branch and total is their sum; indices never move backward.
Edge cases: If no candidate fits, the answer is empty. Positive candidates ensure totals grow, bounding recursion depth by target divided by the smallest candidate.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. Search time is exponential in the worst case; recursion/path space depends on maximum combination length, excluding output.

Task and constraints: Given an array of distinct integers candidates and a target integer target, return a list of all unique combinations of candidates where the chosen numbers sum to target. You may return the combinations in any order. Inputs and required output follow the stated problem constraints.
Idea: Sorts candidates, then recursively chooses values that fit the remaining target. It copies the path at target zero, recurses from the same index to allow reuse, and pops each choice afterward.
Technique and why it applies: Sorted backtracking keeps combinations ordered and prunes values larger than the remaining target.
Invariant: The path sum plus remaining target stays equal to the original target; the start index never moves backward.
Edge cases: Positive candidates make totals increase; target zero records an empty path. Sorting adds O(n log n), recursion depth depends on target/minimum candidate.
Complexity: The author labels O(k*n^k) time and O(k) space; this is a rough search bound, not a tight bound for every input. Output storage is additional.

Task and constraints: Given a collection of candidate numbers (candidates) and a target number (target), find all unique combinations in candidates where the candidate numbers sum to target. Inputs and required output follow the stated problem constraints.
Idea: Candidates are sorted and DFS explores suffixes. It stops when the sum reaches target, skips equal adjacent values at each depth, and recurses on nums[i+1:] with a newly built path.
Technique and why it applies: Sorted backtracking enumerates subsets; same-depth duplicate skipping avoids duplicate combinations, and suffixes prevent reusing an occurrence.
Invariant: curr is the selected sorted combination and summ is its sum; recursive calls only see later positions.
Edge cases: Equal values may both be chosen from distinct positions, but redundant same-depth branches are skipped. Suffix slicing copies lists.
Complexity: No label was supplied. Search is exponential in the worst case; sorting is O(n log n), and suffix copies add costs. Auxiliary space can be O(n), excluding output.

Task and constraints: Given a collection of candidate numbers (candidates) and a target number (target), find all unique combinations in candidates where the candidate numbers sum to target. Inputs and required output follow the stated problem constraints.
Idea: After sorting, the helper loops from start while a value fits the remaining target. It skips repeated values at the same depth, recurses from start+1, and copies the path at target zero.
Technique and why it applies: Sorted backtracking with same-depth duplicate skipping finds unique combinations, while start+1 enforces single use of each occurrence.
Invariant: The path contains selected values; target is the remaining sum and start excludes earlier positions.
Edge cases: Duplicates can appear together when at different positions. Positive values make stopping when a value exceeds target safe.
Complexity: The author labels O(k*C(n,k)) time and O(k) space, a simplified search estimate. Sorting adds O(n log n), and output storage is additional.

Task and constraints: Given an unsorted integer array nums, return the smallest missing positive integer. Inputs and required output follow the stated problem constraints.
Idea: A reverse scan collects positive values in a set, tracks their minimum and maximum, and deletes every element from nums. It returns 1 if needed, max+1 if all values through max exist, or searches for a gap.
Technique and why it applies: Hash-set membership makes the gap search efficient, but this variant does not meet constant-extra-space placement.
Invariant: The set contains encountered positive values, while mn and mx track their extremes.
Edge cases: If there are no positives it returns 1. It empties the input list and allocates O(n) extra set space, violating the stated constant-space requirement.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. Expected time is O(n), but auxiliary space is O(n), contrary to the statement.

Task and constraints: Given an unsorted integer array nums, return the smallest missing positive integer. Inputs and required output follow the stated problem constraints.
Idea: Each in-range value is swapped into index value-1 until it is correctly placed or its destination already holds the same value. A final scan finds the first mismatch, or returns n+1.
Technique and why it applies: In-place cyclic placement maps positive values to their corresponding array positions.
Invariant: A value v in [1,n] is moved toward index v-1; the equality guard prevents endless swaps on duplicates.
Edge cases: Nonpositive and oversized values remain out of range; duplicates stop at occupied slots. The input is modified.
Complexity: The author labels O(n) time and O(1) space, consistent with cyclic placement and constant auxiliary variables.

Task and constraints: Given n non-negative integers representing an elevation map where the width of each bar is 1, compute how much water it can trap after raining. Inputs and required output follow the stated problem constraints.
Idea: The code compares endpoint heights and processes the shorter side, updates that side's maximum, adds any deficit below the maximum, then moves the pointer inward.
Technique and why it applies: Two pointers work because the shorter endpoint limits the water level on the side processed.
Invariant: maxl and maxr store processed side maxima, and res totals water at processed positions.
Edge cases: Flat and monotone bars trap zero; equal endpoints process the left side. Input is nonempty by the statement.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. Time is O(n) as pointers move inward; auxiliary space is O(1).

Task and constraints: Given n non-negative integers representing an elevation map where the width of each bar is 1, compute how much water it can trap after raining. Inputs and required output follow the stated problem constraints.
Idea: The code finds a global tallest bar, scans left of it while tracking the highest bar seen, then scans backward from the right endpoint toward the peak with a right-side maximum.
Technique and why it applies: The global peak separates the map into sides where each running maximum determines trapped water.
Invariant: second_top points to the highest bar seen in the current directional scan; each bar adds the gap to that maximum.
Edge cases: A peak at either endpoint leaves one scan empty. The code assumes a nonempty list because it reads A[0].
Complexity: The author labels O(n) time and O(1) space, matching the linear scans and scalar state.

Task and constraints: Given n non-negative integers representing an elevation map where the width of each bar is 1, compute how much water it can trap after raining. Inputs and required output follow the stated problem constraints.
Idea: A right-to-left pass stores the maximum height strictly to each position's right. A left-to-right pass tracks the prefix maximum and adds the nonnegative difference between the lower boundary and current height.
Technique and why it applies: Prefix and suffix maxima provide both boundaries needed to compute water above each bar.
Invariant: left is the maximum through the current position; right[i] is the maximum strictly to its right.
Edge cases: At the final position right is zero, and max(...,0) prevents negative water. Flat or monotone arrays trap none.
Complexity: The author labels O(n) time and O(n) space; two passes are linear and right stores one value per bar.

Task and constraints: Given n non-negative integers representing an elevation map where the width of each bar is 1, compute how much water it can trap after raining. Inputs and required output follow the stated problem constraints.
Idea: A stack stores bar indices. When the current height reaches the top height, bars are popped and water is added in horizontal layers using the popped height and distances between boundaries; then the current index is pushed.
Technique and why it applies: A monotonic stack identifies left and right walls when a taller or equal right boundary arrives.
Invariant: The stack stores unresolved boundary indices in non-increasing height order after popping.
Edge cases: Increasing heights trigger pops; decreasing heights may fill the stack. Equal heights are popped too.
Complexity: The author labels O(n) time and O(n) space. Each index is pushed once and popped at most once; stack size can reach n.

Task and constraints: Given n non-negative integers representing an elevation map where the width of each bar is 1, compute how much water it can trap after raining. Inputs and required output follow the stated problem constraints.
Idea: The code moves the pointer at the shorter endpoint, updates a running level from that bar, and adds level minus its height before continuing inward.
Technique and why it applies: Two pointers process the side whose boundary currently limits the water level.
Invariant: level is the greatest lower-side height processed so far; result sums the deficits.
Edge cases: Flat and monotone arrays add zero water; the code assumes the statement's nonempty input.
Complexity: The author labels O(n) time and O(1) space, consistent with inward pointer movement and scalar variables.

Task and constraints: Given two non-negative integers num1 and num2 represented as strings, return the product of num1 and num2, also represented as a string. Inputs and required output follow the stated problem constraints.
Idea: A result array of length m+n accumulates every digit pair's product and propagates carry to an adjacent position. It then skips leading zero positions and joins the remaining digits.
Technique and why it applies: Grade-school multiplication works digit by digit without converting either entire input.
Invariant: Each result slot accumulates decimal products, with carry propagated to the neighboring digit position.
Edge cases: A zero product returns "0"; individual digit characters are converted, but not the complete input strings.
Complexity: The author labels O(m*n) time and O(m+n) space, matching the nested loops and result buffer.

Task and constraints: Given two non-negative integers num1 and num2 represented as strings, return the product of num1 and num2, also represented as a string. Inputs and required output follow the stated problem constraints.
Idea: The code converts both entire strings to Python integers, multiplies them, and converts the product back to text.
Technique and why it applies: This uses built-in integer multiplication rather than digit-by-digit multiplication.
Invariant: The converted integers represent the decimal values of the inputs.
Edge cases: The output may be numerically correct, but whole-input conversion explicitly violates the statement's rule.
Complexity: The author labels O(m*n) time and O(m+n) space, but that does not describe this implementation; integer multiplication and conversion costs depend on Python's implementation.

Task and constraints: Given an input string (s) and a pattern (p), implement wildcard pattern matching with support for '?' and '*' where: Inputs and required output follow the stated problem constraints.
Idea: A boolean table stores whether each pair of input and pattern prefixes match. Leading stars are initialized; a star uses the left or upper state, while literal/? uses the diagonal state.
Technique and why it applies: Dynamic programming models prefix matches using smaller prefix results.
Invariant: result[i][j] describes whether the first i input characters match the first j pattern characters.
Edge cases: Leading stars may match empty input; literal mismatches remain false. The last cell requires a full match.
Complexity: The author labels O(m*n) time and O(m*n) space when a full table is allocated; the nested loops visit each state.

Task and constraints: Given an input string (s) and a pattern (p), implement wildcard pattern matching with support for '?' and '*' where: Inputs and required output follow the stated problem constraints.
Idea: Two DP rows are used instead of a full matrix. The empty-input row is initialized for leading stars, then each input character's row is computed from the previous row and the current row's left cell.
Technique and why it applies: Rolling-row dynamic programming retains only states needed for the next input prefix.
Invariant: The previous row represents the prior input prefix; the current row is filled left to right and column zero is reset.
Edge cases: Empty input uses the initialized row; an empty pattern cannot match nonempty input. Star can consume zero or more characters.
Complexity: The author labels O(m*n) time and O(n) space, matching the nested loops and two rows.

Task and constraints: Given an input string (s) and a pattern (p), implement wildcard pattern matching with support for '?' and '*' where: Inputs and required output follow the stated problem constraints.
Idea: It recursively matches literals and ? one character at a time. For *, it tries the remaining pattern against successive suffixes of s, including the empty suffix.
Technique and why it applies: Recursive backtracking explores possible lengths assigned to a star.
Invariant: Each call evaluates the remaining suffixes of the input and pattern.
Edge cases: Repeated stars cause repeated work and slicing copies strings. The base case rejects empty s with a nonempty all-star pattern, so this variant mishandles that case.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. Worst-case time is exponential; recursion and slices add overhead and can use O(m+n) stack depth.

Task and constraints: Given an input string (s) and a pattern (p), implement wildcard pattern matching with support for '?' and '*' where: Inputs and required output follow the stated problem constraints.
Idea: It greedily consumes matching literals and ?. At *, it saves the continuation and string position; after mismatch it extends the last star by one character and retries, then skips trailing stars.
Technique and why it applies: Greedy matching with retry at the latest star avoids a full DP table.
Invariant: last_p_ptr stores where matching resumes after the star; last_s_ptr tracks how much input that star covers.
Edge cases: A mismatch without an earlier star fails; empty input matches only remaining stars. The count assertion is an internal bound check.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. The code asserts O(m*n) iterations and uses O(1) auxiliary pointer state.

Task and constraints: Given an array of non-negative integers nums, you are initially positioned at the first index of the array. Inputs and required output follow the stated problem constraints.
Idea: The range [l,r] is the current reachable layer. The code scans it for the farthest next index, advances the next layer to start at r+1, and increments the jump count until r reaches the end.
Technique and why it applies: Greedy range expansion works because scanning the current reachable layer finds the farthest boundary attainable with one more jump.
Invariant: At each iteration, indices through r are reachable within the current jump count, and l..r is the layer scanned.
Edge cases: A one-element array skips the loop and returns zero. The statement guarantees the end is reachable, so the range progresses.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. Time is O(n), since each index is scanned in one layer; auxiliary space is O(1).
